subject: Anatomy
title: Anterior Abdominal Wall
objectives: Identify the key structures of Anterior Abdominal Wall at each level of dissection.
Relate the nerves, vessels and muscles of Anterior Abdominal Wall to their functions.
Localise the named spaces and regions of Anterior Abdominal Wall and list their contents.
Recognise the common clinical lesions associated with Anterior Abdominal Wall.
Reproduce the high-yield relations of Anterior Abdominal Wall tested in vivas and MCQs.

cards.front: Name the layers crossed, in order, by a scalpel entering the peritoneal cavity through the anterior abdominal wall lateral to the rectus and below the umbilicus.
cards.back: Skin, Camper's fatty fascia, Scarpa's membranous fascia, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, fascia transversalis, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum.

cards.front: What is Camper's fascia and where does it continue?
cards.back: The fatty superficial layer of the superficial fascia. It continues into the thigh as ordinary subcutaneous fat and loses its fat in the scrotum, where it becomes the dartos muscle.

cards.front: What is Scarpa's fascia?
cards.back: The deep membranous layer of the superficial fascia of the lower abdominal wall, best defined below the umbilicus and in the midline.

cards.front: Where does Scarpa's fascia attach inferiorly, and what is the surgical consequence?
cards.back: It fuses with the fascia lata of the thigh about one finger-breadth below the inguinal ligament (Holden's line). Fluid deep to it therefore cannot track into the thigh.

cards.front: Which perineal fascia is the direct continuation of Scarpa's fascia?
cards.back: Colles' fascia of the superficial perineal pouch; in the scrotum the same layer becomes the dartos and in the penis Buck's outer covering.

cards.front: Explain the distribution of extravasated urine after rupture of the bulbar urethra in fascial terms.
cards.back: Urine enters the superficial perineal pouch and is contained by Colles' fascia, so it spreads into the scrotum and penis and up the anterior abdominal wall deep to Scarpa's fascia, but never into the thigh because Scarpa's fascia fuses with the fascia lata.

cards.front: Why is there no true deep fascia over the anterior abdominal wall?
cards.back: The wall must distend. A tough investing layer would prevent this, so the membranous layer simply blends with the fascia lata at the thigh and with the aponeurosis of external oblique elsewhere.

cards.front: What is the fascia transversalis?
cards.back: The continuous layer of fascia lining the whole inner surface of the abdominal wall, between the transversus abdominis and the extraperitoneal fat.

cards.front: Name three structures derived from the fascia transversalis.
cards.back: The deep inguinal ring and the internal spermatic fascia, the anterior wall of the femoral sheath, and the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

cards.front: Which surgical plane is the extraperitoneal fat used for, and why is it valuable?
cards.back: It is the plane of totally extraperitoneal (TEP) hernia repair and of extraperitoneal approaches to the bladder, iliac vessels and lumbar sympathetic chain. The peritoneum is never opened, so bowel is not exposed and adhesions are avoided.

cards.front: Define the retropubic space of Retzius.
cards.back: The extraperitoneal space between the pubis and the transversalis fascia anteriorly and the bladder posteriorly, containing fat and the prevesical venous plexus. It is the plane entered for open prostatectomy and for retropubic mesh.

cards.front: What is the space of Bogros?
cards.back: The lateral extension of the retropubic space, between the transversalis fascia and the peritoneum in the iliac fossa. It is the space into which preperitoneal mesh is laid in TEP and TAPP repairs.

cards.front: What is the linea semilunaris?
cards.back: The curved lateral border of the rectus abdominis, where the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles fuse to form the rectus sheath. It runs from the ninth costal cartilage to the pubic tubercle.

cards.front: Where does a Spigelian hernia occur and why is it easily missed?
cards.back: Through the Spigelian fascia at the junction of the linea semilunaris with the arcuate line, lateral to the rectus. The sac spreads deep to the intact external oblique aponeurosis, so there is often no visible lump - it is an interstitial hernia.

cards.front: Which layers form the umbilicus?
cards.back: Skin adherent to a fibrous cicatrix, the fused linea alba and transversalis fascia, and peritoneum. There is no fat and no muscle, which is why it is a congenital weak point.

cards.front: Which three fibrous cords converge on the deep surface of the umbilicus?
cards.back: The ligamentum teres (obliterated left umbilical vein) above, and the median umbilical ligament (urachus) with the two medial umbilical ligaments (obliterated umbilical arteries) below.

cards.front: External oblique - origin.
cards.back: The outer surfaces of the lower eight ribs, interdigitating with serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi.

cards.front: External oblique - insertion.
cards.back: The anterior half of the iliac crest, and by aponeurosis into the linea alba, pubic crest and pubic tubercle.

cards.front: External oblique - nerve supply.
cards.back: The anterior rami of T7 to T11 (thoraco-abdominal nerves) and the subcostal nerve T12.

cards.front: External oblique - direction of fibres and its surgical use.
cards.back: Downwards, forwards and medially - the hands-in-pockets direction. The aponeurosis is opened along this line in a groin incision so that it can be closed as a strong flap.

cards.front: Internal oblique - origin.
cards.back: The thoracolumbar fascia, the anterior two-thirds of the iliac crest and the lateral two-thirds of the inguinal ligament.

cards.front: Internal oblique - insertion.
cards.back: The lower three or four costal cartilages, the linea alba, and through the conjoint tendon into the pubic crest and pectineal line.

cards.front: Internal oblique - nerve supply.
cards.back: T7 to T12 plus the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1).

cards.front: Internal oblique - direction of fibres.
cards.back: Upwards, forwards and medially, at right angles to external oblique; its lowest fibres arch over the cord and become the conjoint tendon.

cards.front: Transversus abdominis - origin.
cards.back: The inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages, the thoracolumbar fascia, the anterior two-thirds of the iliac crest and the lateral third of the inguinal ligament.

cards.front: Transversus abdominis - insertion.
cards.back: The linea alba and, with the internal oblique, the conjoint tendon to the pubic crest and pectineal line.

cards.front: Transversus abdominis - nerve supply.
cards.back: T7 to T12 with the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1).

cards.front: Transversus abdominis - action.
cards.back: It is the main compressor of the abdominal contents and the deep corset of the wall; its arching lower fibres produce the shutter mechanism of the inguinal canal.

cards.front: Rectus abdominis - origin.
cards.back: The pubic crest, pubic tubercle and the front of the pubic symphysis.

cards.front: Rectus abdominis - insertion.
cards.back: The fifth, sixth and seventh costal cartilages and the xiphoid process.

cards.front: Rectus abdominis - nerve supply.
cards.back: The anterior rami of T7 to T12, which enter the lateral edge of the sheath - so a vertical paramedian incision that retracts the muscle laterally preserves them.

cards.front: Rectus abdominis - action.
cards.back: Flexion of the trunk, elevation of the pelvis and increase of intra-abdominal pressure in straining, coughing and expulsive efforts.

cards.front: Describe the tendinous intersections of rectus abdominis and their surgical importance.
cards.back: There are usually three, at the xiphoid, the umbilicus and midway between. They adhere firmly to the anterior sheath but not to the posterior sheath, so a rectus sheath haematoma is limited anteriorly in compartments but can track freely behind the muscle.

cards.front: Pyramidalis - attachments, nerve and surgical value.
cards.back: From the pubic crest to the linea alba, supplied by the subcostal nerve (T12). Its apex points to the midline, so it is a reliable guide to the linea alba in a Pfannenstiel incision.

cards.front: What is the conjoint tendon and what does it form?
cards.back: The fused aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis, inserting into the pubic crest and the medial part of the pectineal line. It reinforces the medial part of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

cards.front: What happens when the conjoint tendon is weak or wide?
cards.back: The medial part of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal loses support, and a direct inguinal hernia bulges through Hesselbach's triangle.

cards.front: What is the inguinal ligament and between which points does it run?
cards.back: The thickened, in-rolled lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. It forms the floor of the inguinal canal.

cards.front: Describe the lacunar ligament of Gimbernat.
cards.back: The triangular medial expansion of the inguinal ligament onto the pecten pubis. It forms the sharp medial boundary of the femoral ring and is the structure divided to release a strangulated femoral hernia.

cards.front: What is the pectineal ligament of Cooper and which repair uses it?
cards.back: The strong periosteal ridge along the pecten pubis, the lateral continuation of the lacunar ligament. It is the anchoring structure of the McVay repair for femoral and large direct hernias.

cards.front: Cremaster muscle - origin and nerve supply.
cards.back: Loops of muscle derived from the lower border of the internal oblique, supplied by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2).

cards.front: What is the afferent and efferent pathway of the cremasteric reflex?
cards.back: Afferent by the ilioinguinal nerve from the upper medial thigh, efferent by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve to the cremaster. Both are L1 and L2.

cards.front: Describe the rectus sheath above the costal margin.
cards.back: The anterior wall is the external oblique aponeurosis only. There is no posterior wall - the muscle lies directly on the fifth to seventh costal cartilages.

cards.front: Describe the rectus sheath between the costal margin and the arcuate line.
cards.back: The internal oblique aponeurosis splits. The anterior wall is external oblique plus the anterior lamina of internal oblique; the posterior wall is the posterior lamina of internal oblique plus transversus abdominis and the fascia transversalis.

cards.front: Describe the rectus sheath below the arcuate line.
cards.back: All three aponeuroses pass in front of the muscle. The posterior wall is only fascia transversalis, extraperitoneal fat and peritoneum.

cards.front: Where is the arcuate line of Douglas?
cards.back: About midway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis, roughly a hand's breadth below the umbilicus. It is the curved free lower border of the posterior rectus sheath.

cards.front: What happens to the inferior epigastric vessels at the arcuate line?
cards.back: They pierce the fascia transversalis and enter the sheath below the arcuate line, then run upwards on the deep surface of the rectus to anastomose with the superior epigastric artery.

cards.front: List the contents of the rectus sheath.
cards.back: Rectus abdominis and pyramidalis, the superior and inferior epigastric vessels, the terminal parts of the lower six thoracic nerves with their vessels, and lymphatics.

cards.front: Why does a lower midline incision expose peritoneum more quickly than an upper one?
cards.back: Below the arcuate line there is no aponeurotic posterior sheath, so after the linea alba only transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat and peritoneum separate the surgeon from the cavity.

cards.front: What is the linea alba?
cards.back: The midline raphe formed by the decussating aponeurotic fibres of the three flat muscles of both sides, extending from the xiphoid to the pubic symphysis.

cards.front: Why is the linea alba the chosen line for a midline laparotomy, and what is the price?
cards.back: It is avascular and free of nerves and muscle, so entry is quick and bloodless and can be extended from xiphoid to pubis. The price is a relatively poorly vascularised aponeurotic closure with a higher rate of burst abdomen and incisional hernia than a transverse wound.

cards.front: Where is the linea alba widest and what condition results?
cards.back: Above the umbilicus. Widening there produces divarication of the recti, a midline bulge on straining with no true defect, hernia sac or risk of strangulation.

cards.front: What is an epigastric hernia and what does it usually contain?
cards.back: A protrusion through a defect in the linea alba between the xiphoid and the umbilicus. It usually contains only extraperitoneal fat, and pain is out of proportion to the small size of the lump.

cards.front: Which vessel usually bleeds in a rectus sheath haematoma?
cards.back: The inferior epigastric artery or one of its branches, torn by sudden violent contraction of the rectus, by coughing, or by an injection or trocar.

cards.front: Why can a rectus sheath haematoma below the arcuate line be much larger and mimic an acute abdomen?
cards.back: There is no aponeurotic posterior sheath below the arcuate line, so blood tracks freely into the extraperitoneal space of the pelvis instead of being confined by the sheath.

cards.front: What is Fothergill's sign?
cards.back: A tender abdominal mass that does not cross the midline and stays palpable when the rectus is tensed by lifting the head. It indicates a rectus sheath haematoma rather than an intraperitoneal mass.

cards.front: Why should a stoma be brought out through the rectus muscle?
cards.back: The rectus and its sheath splint the trephine and reduce parastomal herniation, and the site stays clear of the costal margin, iliac crest, umbilicus and belt line.

cards.front: In which plane do the nerves and vessels of the abdominal wall run?
cards.back: The neurovascular plane between the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis - the same plane infiltrated in a transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block.

cards.front: Which segmental nerve supplies the skin over the xiphisternum, the umbilicus and just above the pubis?
cards.back: T7 at the xiphisternum, T10 at the umbilicus, and L1 just above the pubis and over the groin.

cards.front: Which nerve is at risk in a grid-iron incision placed too medially or too low, and what is the result?
cards.back: The iliohypogastric nerve. Division denervates the conjoint tendon, and the weakened posterior wall may later give a direct inguinal hernia on that side.

cards.front: Describe the course of the ilioinguinal nerve in the inguinal canal.
cards.back: It pierces the internal oblique, enters the canal without passing through the deep ring, runs in front of the spermatic cord and leaves through the superficial ring.

cards.front: What is lost when the ilioinguinal nerve is divided at hernia repair?
cards.back: Sensation over the root of the penis and upper scrotum or labium majus and the adjacent medial thigh, plus part of the motor supply to the conjoint tendon. Entrapment in a suture or in mesh instead gives chronic inguinodynia.

cards.front: Which artery supplies the upper anterior abdominal wall, and from where does it arise?
cards.back: The superior epigastric artery, the terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery, entering the sheath between the sternal and costal slips of the diaphragm.

cards.front: From where does the inferior epigastric artery arise?
cards.back: From the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament, medial to the deep inguinal ring.

cards.front: Where is the watershed of the anterior abdominal wall blood supply?
cards.back: At the level of the umbilicus, where the superior and inferior epigastric arteries anastomose within the rectus sheath.

cards.front: Which vessel is the pedicle of a TRAM flap and of a DIEP flap?
cards.back: The deep inferior epigastric artery and vein. The TRAM carries the rectus with it, while the DIEP dissects the perforators out of the muscle and spares it, reducing later abdominal wall weakness.

cards.front: Which superficial arteries cross the lower abdominal wall and from which trunk?
cards.back: The superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac and superficial external pudendal arteries, all from the femoral artery in the femoral triangle.

cards.front: What is the surgical rule for lateral port placement in laparoscopy, in terms of the inferior epigastric artery?
cards.back: Place lateral ports lateral to the linea semilunaris, or transilluminate and inspect the peritoneum from inside - the artery lies in the lateral umbilical fold, so a port placed just lateral to that fold is the one that bleeds.

cards.front: Name the five peritoneal folds seen on the inner surface of the lower abdominal wall.
cards.back: One median umbilical fold (urachus), two medial umbilical folds (obliterated umbilical arteries) and two lateral umbilical folds (inferior epigastric vessels).

cards.front: Which fossae lie between the umbilical folds and what herniates through each?
cards.back: The supravesical fossa (supravesical hernia), the medial inguinal fossa which corresponds to Hesselbach's triangle (direct hernia) and the lateral inguinal fossa at the deep ring (indirect hernia).

cards.front: How does the venous drainage of the abdominal wall divide at the umbilicus?
cards.back: Above the umbilicus to the axillary vein through the lateral thoracic and thoraco-epigastric veins, below the umbilicus to the femoral vein through the superficial epigastric vein.

cards.front: How is the direction of flow in dilated abdominal wall veins used to separate caput medusae from inferior vena caval obstruction?
cards.back: In caput medusae the flow radiates away from the umbilicus in all directions. In caval obstruction the dilated veins are more lateral and flow is upwards below the umbilicus, carrying blood from the femoral to the axillary system.

cards.front: How do the lymphatics of the anterior abdominal wall drain?
cards.back: Above the umbilicus to the anterior axillary (pectoral) nodes, below the umbilicus to the superficial inguinal nodes.

cards.front: Which layers does a midline laparotomy divide?
cards.back: Skin, superficial fascia, linea alba, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat and peritoneum. No muscle, nerve or major vessel is cut.

cards.front: What is the anatomical advantage of a paramedian incision?
cards.back: The rectus is retracted laterally rather than cut, so its segmental nerve supply is preserved, and the muscle is interposed between the anterior and posterior sheath suture lines, which strengthens the closure.

cards.front: Describe Kocher's subcostal incision and its principal nerve hazard.
cards.back: An oblique muscle-cutting incision about one inch below and parallel to the costal margin, dividing the rectus and its sheaths medially. The eighth, ninth and tenth intercostal nerves are at risk, giving numbness or a bulge of the wall.

cards.front: How is a McBurney grid-iron incision placed?
cards.back: At right angles to the spino-umbilical line, centred on the junction of its lateral third with the medial two-thirds - McBurney's point - about 5 to 6 cm long.

cards.front: Why is the grid-iron incision called muscle-splitting?
cards.back: The external oblique aponeurosis is opened along its fibres, then the internal oblique and transversus are split along their own fibre directions rather than cut, so the wall closes back on itself and is strong.

cards.front: What is a Lanz incision?
cards.back: A transverse skin-crease variant of the grid-iron placed in a Langer line at the same point, more cosmetic but with a greater risk to the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.

cards.front: Describe the Pfannenstiel incision layer by layer.
cards.back: A transverse curved skin incision about two finger-breadths above the symphysis, the anterior rectus sheath divided transversely and dissected off the recti, the recti separated in the midline, then the peritoneum opened vertically.

cards.front: Why is a Pfannenstiel incision strong and cosmetic?
cards.back: It lies in a Langer line, and the transverse sheath incision is at right angles to the pull of the recti, so tension on the suture line is minimal and coughing is tolerated.

cards.front: Why do transverse incisions burst less often than vertical ones?
cards.back: Their line runs with the direction of the aponeurotic fibres and the Langer lines, and the pull of the abdominal muscles is across the suture line rather than along it.

cards.front: Which layer of the abdominal wall is the strongest and must be closed soundly?
cards.back: The linea alba or the anterior rectus sheath. Its secure closure is what holds the wound together; the peritoneum regenerates and need not be closed.

cards.front: State the standard technical rule for mass closure of a midline wound.
cards.back: A continuous non-absorbable monofilament such as polypropylene, bites of about 1 cm from the fascial edge placed about 1 cm apart, and a suture length to wound length ratio of at least 4 to 1, tied without tension.

cards.front: Define burst abdomen and its partial form.
cards.back: Disruption of an abdominal wound in the early postoperative period. In the partial form the deep layers separate with intact skin, which is the way most incisional hernias begin; in the complete form the wound gapes and prolapse of bowel is called evisceration.

cards.front: Which layers are crossed by a supra-umbilical port and why is it the standard site?
cards.back: Skin, linea alba, transversalis fascia and peritoneum - no muscle and no major vessel, and the wall is thinnest and closest to the peritoneum there.

cards.front: Where is Palmer's point and when is it used?
cards.back: In the left mid-clavicular line about 3 cm below the costal margin, used for the initial entry when periumbilical adhesions are expected. It avoids the usual site of adhesions and is remote from the aorta.

cards.front: Why does a Rutherford Morison incision give good access to the right iliac fossa and the iliac vessels?
cards.back: It is an oblique muscle-cutting extension of the grid-iron running upwards and laterally towards the iliac crest; it opens the whole iliac fossa and can be taken extraperitoneally for renal transplantation.

cards.cloze: The membranous layer of the superficial fascia is {{c1::Scarpa's fascia}}, which fuses with the fascia lata one finger-breadth below the inguinal ligament.
In the perineum, Scarpa's fascia continues as {{c1::Colles' fascia}}, which is why extravasated urine reaches the scrotum but not the thigh.
A Spigelian hernia protrudes at the junction of the linea semilunaris with the {{c1::arcuate line}}.
The conjoint tendon is formed by the fused aponeuroses of {{c1::internal oblique and transversus abdominis}}.
The inguinal ligament runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the {{c1::pubic tubercle}}.
The sharp medial boundary of the femoral ring is the {{c1::lacunar ligament of Gimbernat}}.
Below the arcuate line the posterior wall of the rectus sheath consists only of {{c1::fascia transversalis, extraperitoneal fat and peritoneum}}.
The arcuate line lies about {{c1::midway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis}}.
The tendinous intersections of the rectus adhere to the {{c1::anterior}} wall of the sheath only.
The dermatome of the umbilicus is {{c1::T10}}.
The nerves of the abdominal wall run in the plane between {{c1::internal oblique and transversus abdominis}}.
The inferior epigastric artery arises from the {{c1::external iliac artery}} just above the inguinal ligament.
The lateral umbilical fold is raised by the {{c1::inferior epigastric vessels}}.
Lymph from the abdominal wall above the umbilicus drains to the {{c1::axillary}} nodes.
McBurney's point lies at the junction of the {{c1::lateral third and medial two-thirds}} of the line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.
For mass closure the suture length to wound length ratio should be at least {{c1::4 to 1}}.

cards.front: Name the four planes that divide the abdomen into nine regions.
cards.back: Two vertical midclavicular (lateral) planes, and two horizontal planes - the subcostal plane through the lowest point of the tenth costal cartilage and the transtubercular plane through the tubercles of the iliac crests at L5.

cards.front: Where is the transpyloric plane of Addison and what lies in it?
cards.back: Midway between the suprasternal notch and the pubic symphysis, at the level of L1 and the tip of the ninth costal cartilage. It contains the pylorus, the neck of the pancreas, the origin of the superior mesenteric artery and portal vein, the duodenojejunal flexure, the hila of the kidneys and the fundus of the gallbladder.

cards.front: Where is the supracristal plane and what does it mark?
cards.back: The line joining the highest points of the iliac crests, at the level of L4. It marks the aortic bifurcation and is the landmark for lumbar puncture.

cards.front: Give the surface marking of the gallbladder fundus.
cards.back: Where the lateral border of the right rectus crosses the ninth costal cartilage - the tip of the ninth cartilage in the transpyloric plane, which is the point of maximal tenderness in Murphy's sign.

cards.front: Give the surface marking of the spleen.
cards.back: Deep to the ninth to eleventh ribs on the left, with its long axis along the tenth rib; it must enlarge to about three times its size before it becomes palpable below the left costal margin.

cards.front: Why does an enlarging spleen appear towards the right iliac fossa?
cards.back: It enlarges along the axis of the tenth rib, downwards, forwards and medially, keeping its notched anterior border palpable - which distinguishes it from a renal mass that enlarges vertically and is ballottable.

cards.front: Which surface landmark marks the deep inguinal ring on abdominal examination?
cards.back: A point half an inch above the mid-inguinal point, immediately above the femoral pulse.

cards.front: What is the anatomical difference between an umbilical and a paraumbilical hernia?
cards.back: A true umbilical hernia protrudes through the umbilical cicatrix itself and is the infantile type. A paraumbilical hernia protrudes through the linea alba immediately above or below the umbilicus, so the umbilicus is stretched into a crescent and the sac has a narrow fibrous neck.

cards.front: Why does an infantile umbilical hernia usually resolve but an adult paraumbilical hernia does not?
cards.back: The infantile defect closes as the rectus muscles approximate and the cicatrix contracts with growth. The adult defect is a fixed fibrous ring in the linea alba under continuing intra-abdominal pressure, so it enlarges and its narrow neck predisposes to obstruction and strangulation.

cards.front: What is an incisional hernia and through which layer does it occur?
cards.back: Herniation through the aponeurotic layer of a previous surgical wound, usually after partial disruption of the linea alba or rectus sheath; the skin and subcutaneous layers remain intact so the sac is covered only by scarred fascia and skin.

cards.front: Why is an incisional hernia often multi-loculated and wide-necked?
cards.back: The fascial defect is irregular with several separate gaps bridged by scar, and adhesions divide the sac into compartments; the wide neck makes strangulation less likely but reduction less complete.

cards.front: Give the boundaries of the inferior lumbar triangle of Petit.
cards.back: The iliac crest below, latissimus dorsi medially and the external oblique laterally, with the internal oblique in its floor.

cards.front: Give the boundaries of the superior lumbar triangle of Grynfeltt.
cards.back: The twelfth rib and serratus posterior inferior above, quadratus lumborum medially and the internal oblique laterally, with the transversalis fascia in its floor. It is the commoner site of a lumbar hernia.

cards.front: What is a divarication of the recti and why is it not repaired as a hernia?
cards.back: A widening of the linea alba with separation of the recti but no fascial defect; there is no sac, no neck and no risk of strangulation, so it is a cosmetic and functional problem only.

cards.front: What is exomphalos and how does it differ anatomically from gastroschisis?
cards.back: In exomphalos the viscera herniate into the base of the umbilical cord and are covered by a sac of amnion and peritoneum, with the cord inserting on the sac. In gastroschisis there is a full-thickness defect of the abdominal wall usually to the right of a normally inserted cord, and the bowel is uncovered and exposed to amniotic fluid.

cards.front: Which nerves are blocked by a transversus abdominis plane block and which incisions does it cover?
cards.back: The anterior rami of T7 to L1 as they run in the neurovascular plane between internal oblique and transversus, giving analgesia to the anterolateral wall for transverse and grid-iron incisions and for stoma sites.

cards.front: Which nerves does a rectus sheath block target and why is it useful for a midline wound?
cards.back: The terminal branches of the lower intercostal nerves as they pierce the posterior wall of the sheath and run behind the rectus, so local anaesthetic deposited between the muscle and the posterior sheath covers the midline incision.

cards.front: Why does a paramedian incision cause less denervation than a Battle pararectal incision?
cards.back: A paramedian incision retracts the rectus laterally and enters medial to its nerve supply. A pararectal incision cuts through the lateral edge of the sheath where the nerves enter, denervating the medial part of the muscle and inviting an incisional hernia.

cards.front: Which structure limits how far a Kocher incision can be extended medially?

cards.back: The defect in the aponeurosis is large enough to admit omentum or bowel, and a port-site Richter's hernia may strangulate a knuckle of bowel with no obvious external lump.

mcqs.stem: A young man falls astride a bar and ruptures his bulbar urethra. Over the next hours his scrotum, penis and lower abdominal wall become swollen and discoloured, but the thighs are spared. Which anatomical fact explains the sparing of the thighs?

mcqs.stem: Which single technical factor most reliably reduces the risk of burst abdomen after a midline laparotomy?

options.text: Closing the peritoneum as a separate layer
options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

options.text: Using absorbable braided suture for the sheath
options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

options.text: Mass closure with a suture length to wound length ratio of at least 4 to 1
options.why:
Key - C) Mass closure with a suture length to wound length ratio of at least 4 to 1. Mass closure with adequate bites and a suture to wound length ratio of at least 4 to 1 distributes tension and is the single best established protection against disruption.

Why the others fail:
A) Closing the peritoneum as a separate layer - The peritoneum regenerates within days and contributes nothing to the strength of the closure.
B) Using absorbable braided suture for the sheath - Rapidly absorbed braided material loses strength before the aponeurosis has healed and is a recognised cause of disruption.
D) Bringing the drain out through the main wound - A drain through the main wound weakens it and increases the risk of both infection and disruption.

mcqs.stem: A balloon dissector is advanced in the plane behind the rectus during a totally extraperitoneal repair. Which anatomical feature allows the dissector to enter the preperitoneal space of Bogros without opening the peritoneum?

options.text: The posterior rectus sheath is absent below the arcuate line, leaving only transversalis fascia between the muscle and the peritoneum
options.why:
Key - A) The posterior rectus sheath is absent below the arcuate line, leaving only transversalis fascia between the muscle and the peritoneum. Why the others fail:
B) The linea alba is deficient below the umbilicus - The linea alba is continuous to the pubic symphysis and is not deficient; it is the posterior sheath, not the midline, that ends at the arcuate line.
C) The peritoneum is adherent to the transversalis fascia only above the arcuate line - The peritoneum is separated from the transversalis fascia by extraperitoneal fat throughout; adherence is not the relevant variable.
D) The inferior epigastric vessels lie behind the peritoneum at this level - The inferior epigastric vessels lie between the transversalis fascia and the peritoneum, and they are a structure to be preserved during the dissection rather than the reason it is possible.

mcqs.stem: A patient returns four days after a Pfannenstiel incision with numbness over the mons and a bulge of the lower lateral abdominal wall on straining. Which single lesion explains both findings?

options.text: Division of the ilioinguinal nerve alone
options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

options.text: Division of the iliohypogastric nerve at the lateral end of the incision
options.why:
Key - B) Division of the iliohypogastric nerve at the lateral end of the incision. The iliohypogastric nerve is both sensory to the suprapubic skin and motor to the lower internal oblique and transversus, so division at the lateral limit of a transverse incision gives numbness with a denervation bulge.

Why the others fail:
A) Division of the ilioinguinal nerve alone - The ilioinguinal nerve is sensory to the mons and upper labium but its loss alone does not weaken enough muscle to produce a bulge of the lateral wall.
C) Transection of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh - The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh is purely sensory to the lateral thigh and supplies no abdominal muscle.
D) Injury to the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve - The genital branch supplies cremaster and a small area of skin, and its injury causes a lost cremasteric reflex rather than an abdominal bulge.

mcqs.stem: A patient with tense ascites and a previous long midline scar needs paracentesis. Which of the following is the soundest anatomical reasoning for the site chosen?

options.text: Midline below the umbilicus, since the linea alba is avascular
options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

options.text: Left lower quadrant lateral to the rectus sheath, since it is lateral to the inferior epigastric artery and away from adhesions under the old scar
options.why:
Key - B) Left lower quadrant lateral to the rectus sheath, since it is lateral to the inferior epigastric artery and away from adhesions under the old scar. A point in the left lower quadrant lateral to the rectus is lateral to the inferior epigastric artery, distant from the midline adhesions, and overlies a usually empty descending colon.

Why the others fail:
A) Midline below the umbilicus, since the linea alba is avascular - The linea alba is avascular but lies directly under the old scar, where bowel is likely to be adherent, and the urachus and a full bladder are additional hazards.
C) Right lower quadrant at McBurney's point, since the caecum is mobile - The caecum is gas-filled and thin-walled and is the structure most easily punctured at McBurney's point.
D) Right hypochondrium, since the liver falls away in ascites - The liver enlarges rather than falls away in many causes of ascites, and the right hypochondrium risks liver and gallbladder.
